reasons: Lake identity gives case_name United States v. Mendenhall, court U.S. Supreme Court, year 1980, and date_decided 1980-06-30.
Lake citations list official 446 U.S. 544, parallel cites 100 S. Ct. 1870 and 64 L. Ed. 2d 497, and vendor-neutral 1980 U.S. LEXIS 102.
The opinion directly addresses when a person is seized within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.
The text states that a person is seized only when physical force or show of authority restrains freedom of movement, and applies that seizure-of-person rule to the airport encounter.
residual_risks: The Key — Anchor label is editorial rather than a verbatim label in the opinion, but the doctrinal fit is supported.

defect.evidence_quote: The Chief Justice, Mr. Justice Blachmun, and Mr. Justice Powell also join all but Part II-A of this opinion.
defect.locator_note: content_page.md frontmatter holding; text page 554 / paragraph b612-6; footnote dagger paragraph b604-13; lake treatment.scope_note.
defect.problem: The free-to-leave proposition is textually supported, but calling it the case holding without a plurality caveat overstates Mendenhall itself. Part II-A was joined only by Justice Rehnquist, and the lake scope note says the formulation was later adopted by the full Court.
defect.proposed_fix: Revise the holding field to state that Justice Stewart's Part II-A opinion announced the free-to-leave benchmark, and that the formulation was later adopted by the full Court as the governing standard.

reasons: The text supports the benchmark: a person is seized only if, in view of all circumstances, a reasonable person would believe he was not free to leave.
The disclosed footnote and lake scope note require a caveat that the formulation was announced in Justice Stewart's opinion and later adopted by the full Court.
residual_risks: Separate concurrence texts are not disclosed in text/, so the vote-count caveat rests on the lead-opinion footnote and lake scope note.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use 'Justice Stewart's plurality formulation, later adopted by the full Court' rather than unqualified 'holding' for the free-to-leave benchmark.
